cas-ecgc-001.question: Geriatric day hospital. An 84-year-old woman reports fatigue and two falls without loss of consciousness over the past month. Medication: bisoprolol 10 mg (started for palpitations), ivabradine 5 mg twice daily added by her GP to "control the heart better", and donepezil. BP 128/70 mmHg. Here is her resting tracing. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Implant a rate-responsive dual-chamber pacemaker straight away
Perform an atropine test to assess sinus node reserve
Stop ivabradine, reduce bisoprolol and reassess with a Holter
Switch bisoprolol to verapamil, which is better tolerated
commentaires: Incorrect: pacing is not indicated while a reversible (here drug-induced) cause has not been corrected, unless the drug is essential and has no alternative.
Incorrect: a pharmacological test adds nothing while the rate-slowing drugs are still on board and does not alter immediate management.
Correct: sinus bradycardia at 38 bpm on three sinus-slowing drugs (beta-blocker, ivabradine, cholinesterase inhibitor): the iatrogenic cause must be removed first, then the rhythm reassessed.
Incorrect: verapamil also depresses sinus node automaticity and AV nodal conduction; it would replace one rate-slowing drug with another.
cas-ecgc-001.explication: The tracing shows sinus P waves, each followed by a narrow QRS after a normal PR interval, at about 38 bpm: sinus bradycardia without AV conduction disturbance. In this patient three drugs slow the sinus node: full-dose bisoprolol, ivabradine (an If current inhibitor whose combination with a beta-blocker predisposes to bradycardia) and donepezil, whose vagal effect is a classic cause of bradycardia and falls in older people. The first step is therefore to stop ivabradine and reduce the beta-blocker, then reassess clinically and with a Holter. If symptomatic bradycardia persists off rate-slowing drugs, or if such a drug is essential with no alternative, pacing becomes justified. Verapamil or diltiazem are not an alternative: they also slow the sinus node.
cas-ecgc-001.aRetenir: Sinus bradycardia on rate-slowing drugs: correct the reversible cause before considering a pacemaker.
cas-ecgc-001.rappel: Sinus node dysfunction comprises sinus bradycardia, pauses or SA block, sometimes with chronotropic incompetence or atrial tachyarrhythmias. Before any pacing decision, the 2021 ESC guidelines require a search for and correction of reversible causes: drugs (beta-blockers, ivabradine, rate-slowing calcium channel blockers, digoxin, antiarrhythmic drugs, cholinesterase inhibitors), hypothyroidism, hyperkalaemia and hypothermia. Pacing is indicated (class I) when symptoms are clearly attributable to bradycardia. When a rate-slowing drug is essential and has no alternative, pacing may be offered so that it can be continued.

cas-ecgc-002.question: A 71-year-old man has had three syncopal episodes in one year without prodrome, one causing a wrist fracture. Resting ECG, echocardiogram and 24-hour Holter are normal. In the clinic, right carotid sinus massage reproduces presyncope with pallor; this is the recording. What do you decide?
options: Offer dual-chamber pacing
Prescribe midodrine and counterpressure manoeuvres
Implant a loop recorder to document a spontaneous episode
Perform an EP study before any decision
commentaires: Correct: a sinus pause > 3 s reproducing symptoms during massage, with severe unpredictable syncope after the age of 40: cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome, an indication for pacing.
Incorrect: these measures target the vasodepressor component or syncope with prodrome; they do not correct cardioinhibitory asystole.
Incorrect: the mechanism is already demonstrated by a positive massage reproducing symptoms; waiting for another traumatic syncope is not justified.
Incorrect: an EP study assesses conduction and intrinsic sinus node function; it adds nothing once carotid sinus syndrome has been documented.
cas-ecgc-002.explication: During the massage the P waves disappear abruptly: no P wave and no QRS for about 4 s, then sinus rhythm resumes. This is asystole due to reflex sinus arrest reproducing the symptoms: the definition of cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome (pause > 3 s). In a patient over 40 years of age with severe, unpredictable and injurious syncope, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend dual-chamber pacing (class I, level A) to reduce recurrences. A loop recorder would help if the mechanism were unknown; here it is established. Vasoconstrictor drugs do not correct asystole. Pacing does not protect against the vasodepressor component, which must be looked for (drop in blood pressure during massage).
cas-ecgc-002.aRetenir: Positive carotid sinus massage (pause > 3 s with symptoms) and severe syncope after 40: dual-chamber pacing.
cas-ecgc-002.rappel: Carotid sinus massage is performed after the age of 40, for 10 s on each side, supine then upright, with continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring. It is positive if it reproduces symptoms with a ventricular pause > 3 s (cardioinhibitory form) and/or a fall in systolic BP > 50 mmHg (vasodepressor form). According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, dual-chamber pacing is indicated (class I, level A) in patients over 40 with severe, unpredictable, recurrent reflex syncope associated with a documented asystolic pause (> 3 s symptomatic or > 6 s asymptomatic), cardioinhibitory carotid sinus syndrome, or asystolic syncope on tilt testing. Pacing does not correct the vasodepressor component, which accounts for some recurrences.

cas-ecgc-003.question: Cardiac surgery intensive care unit, day 3 after triple bypass grafting. A 66-year-old man, asymptomatic and haemodynamically stable, on amiodarone since an episode of AF on day 2; epicardial pacing wires are in place. Telemetry records several episodes like this one. What do you propose?
options: Implant a permanent pacemaker before the wires are removed
Stop amiodarone and remove the epicardial wires
Start a continuous isoprenaline infusion for 48 hours
Epicardial backup pacing and prolonged observation
commentaires: Incorrect: early implantation risks an unnecessary device; the ESC recommends observation for 5 days to several weeks.
Incorrect: removing backup pacing during active sinus node dysfunction exposes the patient to prolonged unprotected asystole.
Incorrect: isoprenaline is a bridge for poorly tolerated bradycardia; it is proarrhythmic and unnecessary in a stable patient with pacing wires.
Correct: postoperative sinus node dysfunction is often transient (oedema, pericarditis, amiodarone): an observation period is recommended, covered by backup pacing.
cas-ecgc-003.explication: After a few sinus beats, atrial activity stops: a pause of about 3.6 s with no P wave and no QRS, then sinus rhythm resumes. The pause is not a simple multiple of the sinus cycle: this is sinus arrest. After cardiac surgery this dysfunction is often transient, promoted by oedema, pericarditis, electrolyte disturbances and amiodarone. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend an observation period of 5 days to several weeks before deciding on permanent pacing. The epicardial wires, programmed to backup pacing (for example AAI or DDD at a low rate), protect the patient during that time. Isoprenaline is justified only when no pacing is available in a poorly tolerating patient.
cas-ecgc-003.aRetenir: Sinus node dysfunction after cardiac surgery: observe for 5 days to several weeks with backup pacing before any permanent pacemaker.
cas-ecgc-003.rappel: Sinus arrest: absence of P waves for a period that is not a multiple of the baseline PP cycle; second-degree SA block: a pause that is an exact multiple of the PP cycle. After cardiac surgery or heart transplantation, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend (class I) an observation period of 5 days to several weeks to see whether sinus node dysfunction resolves, and up to 5 days for high-grade AV block. This period can be shortened in complete AV block with no or a slow escape rhythm, which is unlikely to resolve. Epicardial wire thresholds rise within days and must be checked daily.

cas-ecgc-004.question: Arrhythmia clinic. A 76-year-old woman has repeated brief dizzy spells, on no rate-slowing drug; TSH and potassium are normal, and the resting ECG shows a PR of 170 ms with narrow QRS complexes. The Holter records this episode, which coincides with dizziness noted in her diary. Pacing is indicated. Which pacing mode do you choose?
options: VVI at 60 bpm, since AV conduction is normal
DDD with ventricular pacing minimisation
DDD with a short AV delay to guarantee ventricular capture
VDD with a single lead and floating atrial dipole
commentaires: Incorrect: in sinus node dysfunction, ventricular-only pacing causes pacemaker syndrome and more AF than dual-chamber pacing.
Correct: symptomatic sinus node dysfunction: dual-chamber pacing, limiting unnecessary ventricular pacing since AV conduction is normal.
Incorrect: a short AV delay forces permanent and unnecessary ventricular pacing, harmful to ventricular function and increasing AF risk.
Incorrect: VDD does not pace the atrium, so it cannot correct a sinus pause, which remains a ventricular pause.
cas-ecgc-004.explication: The Holter shows a 5-s pause with no P wave and no QRS, then sinus rhythm resumes: symptomatic sinus arrest with symptom–rhythm correlation. AV conduction is normal (PR 170 ms, narrow QRS). The pacing indication is class I. In sinus node dysfunction, dual-chamber pacing is preferred over ventricular-only pacing, which causes pacemaker syndrome and AF. As AV conduction is preserved, an algorithm minimising ventricular pacing should be programmed (AAI–DDD switching or AV search): unnecessary ventricular pacing promotes AF and deterioration of ventricular function. VDD does not pace the atrium and cannot correct a sinus pause.
cas-ecgc-004.aRetenir: Symptomatic sinus node dysfunction with normal AV conduction: DDD with minimisation of ventricular pacing.
cas-ecgc-004.rappel: According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, pacing is indicated (class I) in sinus node dysfunction when symptoms are clearly correlated with bradycardia. Dual-chamber pacing is recommended (class I) over ventricular-only pacing to reduce the risk of AF and stroke, avoid pacemaker syndrome and improve quality of life. In patients with a DDD pacemaker for sinus node dysfunction, minimisation of unnecessary ventricular pacing through programming is recommended. In the SAVE PACe trial, a strategy minimising ventricular pacing reduced the relative risk of persistent AF by about 40%.
cas-ecgc-004.legende: Holter, 3:20 pm: "dizziness" noted by the patient

cas-ecgc-005.question: Cardiology clinic. A 63-year-old man on no medication has had breathlessness and a sensation of "pounding in the neck" on mild exertion for six months. LVEF 60%, no valve disease. This is his resting tracing; on exercise testing the PR stays above 350 ms and the discomfort is reproduced. Which statement is the most accurate?
options: First-degree AV block is never symptomatic
Dual-chamber pacing may be considered
A VVI pacemaker would be enough to relieve these symptoms
Pacing is a class I indication
commentaires: Incorrect: a very long PR places atrial systole against the previous ventricular systole, with loss of atrial contribution and venous backflow.
Correct: marked first-degree AV block (PR > 300 ms) with symptoms resembling pacemaker syndrome, reproduced on exercise: pacing should be considered (class IIa).
Incorrect: VVI pacing does not restore AV synchrony and could even worsen symptoms (pacemaker syndrome).
Incorrect: in symptomatic first-degree AV block, the 2021 ESC guidelines give only a class IIa, level of evidence C.
cas-ecgc-005.explication: Every P wave is conducted, with a constant PR of about 380 ms and narrow QRS complexes: marked first-degree AV block. When the PR exceeds 300 ms, atrial contraction occurs early in diastole, sometimes during the preceding ventricular systole: loss of atrial contribution, backflow into the jugular veins ("pounding in the neck") and sometimes diastolic mitral regurgitation. The picture resembles pacemaker syndrome, hence the term "pseudo-pacemaker syndrome". The 2021 ESC guidelines state that pacing should be considered (class IIa, level C) when symptoms are clearly attributable to first-degree AV block, ideally after reproducing them on exercise. Pacing must preserve AV synchrony (dual-chamber, appropriate AV delay), which VVI does not.
cas-ecgc-005.aRetenir: PR > 300 ms with pacemaker syndrome-like symptoms: dual-chamber pacing should be considered (IIa).
cas-ecgc-005.rappel: First-degree AV block is a PR > 200 ms with conduction of every P wave. It is usually nodal and benign. When the PR exceeds 300 ms, atrial systole may fall during or just after the preceding ventricular systole and reproduce the haemodynamics of pacemaker syndrome. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering pacing (class IIa, C) in patients with persistent symptoms of this kind attributable to first-degree AV block (PR > 300 ms). In the absence of symptoms, isolated first-degree AV block is not an indication for pacing.

cas-ecgc-006.question: Emergency department. A 79-year-old man has increasing fatigue and one presyncopal episode. For three weeks he has been taking bisoprolol 5 mg and slow-release diltiazem 200 mg, combined by two different prescribers for angina. BP 118/72 mmHg, no chest pain, normal troponin. Here is the monitor strip. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Insert a temporary pacing wire as an emergency
Book a dual-chamber pacemaker within the week
Replace diltiazem with digoxin
Stop both AV nodal blockers and monitor
commentaires: Incorrect: the patient is stable and the block is nodal; temporary pacing, which is invasive and not free of complications, is not indicated.
Incorrect: pacing is not indicated for drug-induced block before checking whether it resolves once the drugs are stopped.
Incorrect: digoxin also slows AV nodal conduction and would worsen the block.
Correct: Wenckebach AV block with narrow QRS on two combined AV nodal blocking drugs: a reversible drug-induced cause to correct under monitoring before any pacing.
cas-ecgc-006.explication: The PR lengthens progressively from beat to beat until a P wave is not conducted, then the cycle restarts with a shorter PR: second-degree Mobitz I AV block (4:3 Wenckebach period) with narrow QRS. This block is almost always located in the AV node. The combination of a beta-blocker with a rate-slowing calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil) is a classic cause of nodal block in older patients. As the patient is stable, both drugs should be stopped and the patient monitored on telemetry; temporary pacing is considered only if the rhythm is poorly tolerated or worsens. If the block persists after drug washout, or if these drugs are essential, permanent pacing can then be discussed.
cas-ecgc-006.aRetenir: Narrow-QRS Wenckebach on a beta-blocker plus diltiazem: stop the AV nodal blockers and monitor before talking about a pacemaker.
cas-ecgc-006.rappel: Second-degree Mobitz I AV block is recognised by progressive PR prolongation until a blocked P wave; the PR after the pause is the shortest. With narrow QRS it is almost always nodal and may be physiological in athletes or during sleep. The 2021 ESC guidelines require a reversible cause (drugs, hyperkalaemia, Lyme disease, high vagal tone) to be sought and corrected before permanent pacing is considered; block that persists after correction, or whose causative treatment is essential, does warrant pacing. Combining a beta-blocker with diltiazem or verapamil potentiates the negative dromotropic effect and should be avoided in older patients.

cas-ecgc-007.question: Emergency department. A 77-year-old woman had sudden syncope on getting up from the table, without prodrome, with a scalp laceration. No rate-slowing drugs, normal potassium. On arrival she is conscious, BP 135/80 mmHg. Here is the monitor strip. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Admit and implant a pacemaker promptly
Arrange an outpatient 24-hour Holter before deciding
Give atropine to improve conduction
Perform a tilt test for reflex syncope
commentaires: Correct: Mobitz II AV block with wide QRS after syncope: infranodal block with a high risk of asystole, an indication for permanent pacing without waiting.
Incorrect: the diagnosis is already made, and the risk of complete block without escape rules out discharge without protection.
Incorrect: atropine acts on the AV node; in infranodal block, by accelerating the sinus rate, it can increase the number of blocked P waves.
Incorrect: syncope without prodrome with documented infranodal block points to an arrhythmic cause, not a reflex one.
cas-ecgc-007.explication: The P waves are regular; one P wave in three is not followed by a QRS, while the PR of conducted beats stays constant, including after the pause: second-degree Mobitz II AV block with wide QRS complexes. This block is located below the AV node (His or infra-His); it can progress suddenly to complete block with a slow or absent escape rhythm, which explains syncope without prodrome. Permanent pacing is clearly indicated (class I), with no observation period, in the absence of a reversible cause. Meanwhile the patient must stay on telemetry with transcutaneous pacing available. Atropine is useless, or even harmful, in infranodal block.
cas-ecgc-007.aRetenir: Mobitz II with wide QRS and syncope: permanent pacing without delay; atropine has no role.
cas-ecgc-007.rappel: In second-degree Mobitz II AV block, P waves are blocked unexpectedly while the PR of conducted beats is constant, including after the pause. The block is infranodal, especially with wide QRS complexes, and often progresses to complete block. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) for permanent or paroxysmal Mobitz II, high-grade, infranodal 2:1 or complete AV block, irrespective of symptoms, in the absence of a reversible cause. Atropine, which acts on the AV node, may worsen infranodal block by increasing the sinus rate.

cas-ecgc-008.question: Cardiac intensive care unit. A 69-year-old man, asymptomatic, found incidentally to have this tracing, stable for 12 hours; conducted beats have a PR of 200 ms and narrow QRS complexes. You perform a bicycle exercise test to locate the level of block. Which response most strongly suggests infranodal block?
options: A return to 1:1 conduction with a PR of 180 ms
The appearance of 3:2 Wenckebach periods
A shift to 3:1 conduction as the sinus rate rises on exercise
Persistent 2:1 block with an unchanged PR on exercise
commentaires: Incorrect: improved conduction under adrenergic stimulation is typical of nodal block.
Incorrect: progressive PR prolongation before the blocked P wave reveals nodal block.
Correct: as the atrial rate increases, infranodal block (all-or-none conducting tissue, insensitive to adrenergic tone) lets fewer P waves through.
Incorrect: this response is not discriminating and does not allow the level of block to be determined.
cas-ecgc-008.explication: Every other P wave is conducted, with a constant PR and narrow QRS complexes: 2:1 AV block. In 2:1 block, Mobitz I cannot be distinguished from Mobitz II, since two consecutive PR intervals are never seen. The level of block is clarified by changing autonomic tone. Exercise or atropine speed up the sinus rate and improve nodal conduction: nodal block shifts to 1:1 conduction or Wenckebach periods. Infranodal block is not improved by adrenergic tone: the faster atrial rate increases the proportion of blocked P waves (3:1, 4:1). Conversely, carotid sinus massage worsens nodal block and may improve infranodal block by slowing the sinus rate. Infranodal block requires pacing.
cas-ecgc-008.aRetenir: 2:1 AV block: exercise improves nodal block and worsens infranodal block; carotid sinus massage does the opposite.
cas-ecgc-008.rappel: 2:1 AV block cannot be classified as Mobitz I or Mobitz II on a surface tracing. Features favouring nodal block: narrow QRS, long PR in conducted beats, Wenckebach periods elsewhere on the recording, improvement with exercise or atropine. Features favouring infranodal block: wide QRS, normal PR in conducted beats, worsening on exercise, improvement with carotid sinus massage. When in doubt, an EP study measures the HV interval and locates the block. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in infranodal 2:1 AV block, irrespective of symptoms.

cas-ecgc-009.question: Pre-anaesthetic clinic. An 81-year-old man is scheduled for total knee replacement in ten days. He feels "a bit tired" but has never fainted; no rate-slowing drugs, normal potassium. Here is the tracing recorded in clinic. What do you decide?
options: Operate under general anaesthesia with atropine at hand
Operate under spinal rather than general anaesthesia
Postpone surgery and implant a permanent pacemaker first
Request a Holter and operate if there is no pause > 3 s
commentaires: Incorrect: atropine is ineffective in infranodal block, and anaesthesia exposes the patient to complete block without escape.
Incorrect: spinal anaesthesia can in fact promote bradycardia and hypotension; above all, the pacing indication exists regardless of surgery.
Correct: 2:1 AV block with wide QRS, presumed infranodal: an indication for permanent pacing, to be done before elective surgery.
Incorrect: the absence of pauses over 24 hours does not remove the risk of sudden progression to complete block; the indication rests on the current tracing.
cas-ecgc-009.explication: Every other P wave is blocked; the conducted beats have a constant PR and wide QRS complexes: 2:1 AV block with wide QRS. Although the level of block cannot be proven on a 2:1 pattern, the wide QRS and normal PR of conducted beats strongly suggest infranodal block, with a risk of complete block and a slow escape rhythm. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing in infranodal 2:1 AV block, even without symptoms, when no reversible cause is found. For elective surgery, the right strategy is therefore to implant first, then operate. No anaesthetic technique, and not atropine, protects against infranodal block.
cas-ecgc-009.aRetenir: 2:1 AV block with wide QRS found before elective surgery: pace first, operate afterwards.
cas-ecgc-009.rappel: In 2:1 AV block, the presumed level of block relies on QRS width, the PR of conducted beats and the response to autonomic manoeuvres. A wide QRS with a normal PR suggests infranodal block, whose escape rhythm, if any, is ventricular, slow and unstable. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in infranodal 2:1 AV block, Mobitz II, high-grade and complete AV block, irrespective of symptoms. Perioperatively, a permanent pacing indication found before elective surgery should be dealt with before the operation.

cas-ecgc-010.question: Emergency department, 3 am. An 84-year-old woman presents after a faint; she is drowsy and mottled, BP 72/40 mmHg. No rate-slowing drugs, potassium 4.2 mmol/L. An atropine injection has had no effect. The on-call electrophysiologist will arrive in 45 minutes. Here is the monitor strip. Which measures are appropriate in the meantime? (select all that apply)
options: Lidocaine to suppress the escape rhythm
Continuous isoprenaline infusion
Wait 48 hours to see whether the block resolves
Transcutaneous pacing with analgesia
commentaires: Incorrect: suppressing the ventricular escape rhythm, the patient's only rhythm, would cause asystole.
Correct: while awaiting pacing, isoprenaline can speed up the ventricular escape rhythm and raise blood pressure.
Incorrect: the patient is in shock; no waiting is possible without pacing.
Correct: in a low-output patient, transcutaneous pacing is the bridge to transvenous pacing; capture must be confirmed by palpating a pulse.
cas-ecgc-010.explication: The P waves are regular at about 80 bpm and completely dissociated from regular, slow, wide QRS complexes at about 32 bpm: complete AV block with a ventricular escape rhythm. In this low-output patient atropine is, as expected, ineffective, since the block is infranodal. Guidelines then propose chronotropic catecholamines (isoprenaline or adrenaline) and transcutaneous pacing under analgesia and light sedation, while awaiting a temporary pacing wire or, better, prompt permanent pacing. An escape rhythm must never be suppressed with an antiarrhythmic drug. No observation period is possible when block is poorly tolerated.
cas-ecgc-010.aRetenir: Poorly tolerated complete AV block unresponsive to atropine: isoprenaline and transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to prompt pacing.
cas-ecgc-010.rappel: The ERC 2021 bradycardia algorithm recommends, in the presence of adverse features (shock, syncope, ischaemia, heart failure), atropine 500 µg IV, repeated up to 3 mg. If unsuccessful: isoprenaline (5 µg/min) or adrenaline (2 to 10 µg/min), and transcutaneous pacing, followed by transvenous pacing by an experienced operator. Atropine is often ineffective in wide-QRS infranodal block and in heart transplant recipients. Transcutaneous pacing is painful: it requires analgesia, and mechanical capture must be confirmed at the femoral pulse.

cas-ecgc-011.question: Cardiac surgical ICU, day 2 after surgical aortic valve replacement. A 72-year-old woman, stable, with ventricular epicardial wires in place (threshold 1.5 V). The rhythm has been unchanged since she left theatre. Here is the telemetry after temporarily switching off backup pacing. What is the recommended management?
options: Observe for up to 5 days with backup pacing
Implant a permanent pacemaker today
Remove the wires and wait for conduction to return
Wait at least six weeks before any decision
commentaires: Correct: postoperative complete AV block, well tolerated with a junctional escape: the ESC recommends observation for up to 5 days, as some of these blocks resolve.
Incorrect: in a stable patient with a junctional escape, immediate implantation may prove unnecessary; observation is recommended.
Incorrect: removing protection during complete block would be dangerous; wires are removed once the decision has been made.
Incorrect: this delay applies to some sinus node dysfunction, not to postoperative AV block, for which observation does not exceed 5 days.
cas-ecgc-011.explication: The P waves, regular at about 75 bpm, bear no fixed relationship to regular narrow QRS complexes at about 45 bpm: complete AV block with a junctional escape (narrow QRS, rate 40–60 bpm). After aortic valve surgery the block results from oedema or injury to the His bundle, which lies close to the aortic annulus; it resolves in a proportion of cases. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend a period of clinical observation of up to 5 days to see whether postoperative high-grade or complete AV block resolves. This period can be shortened if the escape rhythm is slow or absent, making resolution unlikely. During observation the epicardial wires keep the patient safe; their threshold must be monitored because it rises within days.
cas-ecgc-011.aRetenir: Well-tolerated complete AV block after cardiac surgery: observe for up to 5 days with backup pacing.
cas-ecgc-011.rappel: The escape rhythm indicates the level of block: junctional (narrow QRS, 40 to 60 bpm, relatively stable) in nodal or high His blocks, ventricular (wide QRS, 20 to 40 bpm, unstable) in infra-His blocks. After cardiac surgery, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend (class I, C) observation for up to 5 days in high-grade or complete AV block; this can be shortened if the escape rhythm is slow or absent. After TAVI, pacing is indicated for complete or high-grade AV block persisting for 24 to 48 hours. Epicardial thresholds rise quickly and do not provide prolonged protection.

cas-ecgc-012.question: Congenital heart disease clinic. A 26-year-old woman with known congenital complete AV block (maternal lupus), entirely asymptomatic, a recreational athlete. Here is her resting tracing. She wants to know whether she needs a pacemaker. Which of the following would make pacing a class I indication for her according to the 2021 ESC guidelines? (select all that apply)
options: Plans for pregnancy
A wide-QRS escape rhythm
Variable PR intervals on the tracing
A mean ventricular rate < 50 bpm
A prolonged QTc interval
commentaires: Incorrect: pregnancy calls for close monitoring but is not in itself a class I indication.
Correct: a wide-QRS escape reflects a lower, less reliable pacemaker focus; it is a risk criterion.
Incorrect: variable PR intervals simply reflect AV dissociation, present by definition in any complete AV block.
Correct: a ventricular rate below 50 bpm is one of the listed risk criteria.
Correct: QTc prolongation exposes the patient to bradycardia-dependent torsades de pointes.
cas-ecgc-012.explication: The P waves (about 90 bpm) are dissociated from regular narrow QRS complexes at about 52 bpm: complete AV block with a junctional escape, the typical appearance of congenital block. In asymptomatic adults, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in the presence of any of the following risk criteria: ventricular dysfunction, prolonged QTc, complex ventricular ectopy, wide-QRS escape rhythm, ventricular rate < 50 bpm, or ventricular pauses longer than three times the escape cycle length. Without any of these criteria, pacing should still be considered (class IIa). Variable PR intervals are inherent to dissociation, and pregnancy is not a criterion in itself.
cas-ecgc-012.aRetenir: Asymptomatic congenital complete AV block: class I if wide QRS, rate < 50 bpm, long QTc, LV dysfunction, complex ventricular ectopy or pauses > 3 escape cycles.
cas-ecgc-012.rappel: Congenital complete AV block, often related to maternal anti-SSA/Ro antibodies, is usually located above the His bundle, hence a narrow-QRS junctional escape. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in symptomatic patients and in asymptomatic patients with any risk criterion: ventricular dysfunction, prolonged QTc, complex ventricular ectopy, wide-QRS escape rhythm, ventricular rate < 50 bpm, or pauses longer than three times the escape cycle length. Without these criteria, pacing should be considered (class IIa). Follow-up includes regular Holter monitoring, exercise testing and echocardiography.

cas-ecgc-013.question: Emergency department, late July. A 34-year-old man who hikes in the Vosges mountains has fatigue and a low-grade fever; an annular erythematous patch on his thigh disappeared ten days ago. He is haemodynamically stable, BP 125/75 mmHg. Here is the monitor strip. What is the most appropriate strategy?
options: A permanent pacemaker before discharge, given his age
High-dose IV corticosteroids for myocarditis
Oral doxycycline at home and review at one month
IV antibiotics, with temporary pacing if poorly tolerated
commentaires: Incorrect: block due to a reversible cause does not justify a permanent pacemaker, which would expose a young man to decades of complications.
Incorrect: Lyme carditis is treated with antibiotics; corticosteroids are not first-line therapy.
Incorrect: complete AV block requires admission with monitoring and initial IV antibiotics.
Correct: probable Lyme carditis: the block, usually nodal, resolves on antibiotics; the patient is protected with temporary pacing if necessary.
cas-ecgc-013.explication: Sinus P waves at about 95 bpm are dissociated from regular narrow QRS complexes at about 48 bpm: complete AV block with a junctional escape. In a young person exposed to ticks with recent erythema migrans, Lyme carditis is the leading diagnosis: the block, usually nodal, can fluctuate rapidly between degrees. Treatment is IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) for inpatients with high-grade block, followed by oral therapy. Conduction returns to normal in the vast majority of cases within days to weeks. Temporary pacing (ideally an active-fixation lead connected to an external generator) is used if the block is poorly tolerated. The 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR guidelines favour temporary pacing over a permanent pacemaker, and the 2021 ESC guidelines list Lyme disease among the reversible causes of AV block.
cas-ecgc-013.aRetenir: Complete AV block in a young person exposed to ticks: think Lyme carditis, treat with antibiotics and avoid a permanent pacemaker.
cas-ecgc-013.rappel: Lyme carditis manifests mainly as AV conduction disturbances, which may fluctuate and progress rapidly and are usually nodal. It should be suspected in high-grade AV block in a young person without heart disease, in an endemic area or after tick exposure. According to the 2020 IDSA/AAN/ACR guidelines, a PR > 300 ms, second- or third-degree AV block or myopericarditis warrants admission with monitoring; treatment is IV ceftriaxone until improvement, then oral therapy (doxycycline, amoxicillin), for a total of 14 to 21 days. The 2021 ESC guidelines list Lyme disease among the reversible causes of AV block, for which permanent pacing is not indicated; temporary pacing may be required.

cas-ecgc-014.question: Syncope clinic. A 74-year-old man has had two brief syncopal episodes without prodrome in three months. The 12-lead ECG shows right bundle branch block with left anterior fascicular block; here is a rhythm strip. LVEF 58%, no ischaemic heart disease, 48-hour Holter unremarkable. What is the recommended next step?
options: A tilt test, as the syncope is probably reflex
An EP study with HV interval measurement
A primary prevention ICD
Simple follow-up, as the Holter was normal
commentaires: Incorrect: the absence of prodrome and the bifascicular block point first to paroxysmal AV block, which must be excluded first.

If the EP study is normal, a loop recorder is recommended. Empirical pacing may be considered in elderly frail patients. If LVEF is ≤ 35%, an ICD or CRT-D should be discussed.

cas-ecgc-015.question: Medical ward, 6 am. The monitor alarm sounds for an 80-year-old man admitted with pneumonia; the nurse finds him unresponsive, with no carotid pulse and no normal breathing. Here is the monitor strip. What is the first action?

Start CPR and give 1 mg of adrenaline as soon as possible
Give 3 mg of atropine before any compressions
Set up transcutaneous pacing before starting compressions
commentaires: Incorrect: asystole is not a shockable rhythm; a shock would delay compressions with no benefit.
Correct: cardiac arrest in a non-shockable rhythm: immediate chest compressions and 1 mg of IV adrenaline as early as possible.
Incorrect: atropine is no longer recommended in cardiac arrest, and nothing should delay compressions.
Incorrect: pacing may be discussed later when P waves are present, but never at the expense of immediate compressions.

A shock is useless. Atropine is no longer recommended in cardiac arrest. The ERC advises checking carefully for P waves whenever asystole is diagnosed, because P-wave asystole may respond to pacing whereas pacing true asystole is useless; pacing must never delay compressions.
cas-ecgc-015.aRetenir: Asystole, even with P waves: immediate CPR and adrenaline; neither shock nor atropine.
cas-ecgc-015.rappel: Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are the non-shockable rhythms of cardiac arrest. According to the ERC 2021 guidelines, high-quality chest compressions are started immediately, 1 mg of adrenaline is given IV or intraosseously as soon as access is obtained and then every 3 to 5 minutes, and reversible causes are sought (4 Hs and 4 Ts). Before concluding that the rhythm is asystole, leads, gain and another lead should be checked so as not to miss fine VF. The ERC advises against pacing asystole without P waves; when P waves are present, pacing may be attempted alongside CPR.

cas-ecgc-016.question: 48-hour Holter report. A 78-year-old woman was referred for spells with falls; resting ECG: sinus rhythm, PR 200 ms, right bundle branch block. During the recording she had a syncope while walking. Here is the corresponding strip (conducted sinus rhythm then resumes). What is your conclusion?

Holter artefact: repeat the recording
Ventricular asystole: EP study before any decision
Symptomatic paroxysmal AV block: permanent pacing indicated
commentaires: Incorrect: this is not a sinus pause, since the P waves continue; it is AV conduction that fails.
Incorrect: the regular P waves are clearly visible and the syncope coincides; an artefact is not credible.
Incorrect: symptom–rhythm correlation is already established; an EP study would add nothing and would delay treatment.
Correct: regular non-conducted P waves with ventricular asystole during syncope: symptomatic paroxysmal AV block, an indication for pacing.
cas-ecgc-016.explication: During the syncope, the tracing shows regular P waves at about 55 bpm that are not followed by any QRS, with no escape rhythm: ventricular asystole due to paroxysmal AV block. The background (right bundle branch block, borderline PR) is consistent with infra-His conduction disease. Symptom–rhythm correlation is established, which is a class I indication for pacing. This is not a sinus pause: in that case the P waves would also disappear. An EP study is unnecessary once symptomatic AV block has been documented.
cas-ecgc-016.aRetenir: Syncope coinciding with non-conducted P waves and no escape: paroxysmal AV block, permanent pacing.
cas-ecgc-016.rappel: Intrinsic paroxysmal AV block occurs in patients with conduction disease (bundle branch block, prolonged HV): it often starts after a premature beat or sinus acceleration, with no escape rhythm for several seconds. It differs from vagal AV block, which is accompanied by simultaneous sinus slowing (lengthening PP intervals) and occurs in a reflex setting. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing (class I) for Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block, whether permanent or paroxysmal. Documentation of symptomatic AV block is enough to establish the indication, without an EP study.

cas-ecgc-017.question: Nephrology unit. A 72-year-old man on haemodialysis via a left-arm arteriovenous fistula, with a history of an infected implantable port. Permanent AF, no rate-slowing drugs for ten days, two presyncopal episodes during dialysis. Here is the tracing. Pacing is indicated. Which solution is the most appropriate?
options: A leadless intracardiac pacemaker
A dual-chamber pacemaker via the left subclavian vein
AV junction ablation followed by observation
A VVI pacemaker via the left cephalic vein
commentaires: Correct: a dialysis patient at high infection risk with venous access to preserve: the typical indication for a leadless pacemaker in VVI(R) mode.
Incorrect: in permanent AF an atrial lead is useless, and the fistula side must be avoided.
Incorrect: AV junction ablation creates pacing dependence; it makes no sense in a patient who is already bradycardic.
Incorrect: the side of the fistula should be avoided (venous stenosis, venous hypertension), and the infection risk of a pocket remains high.
cas-ecgc-017.explication: The tracing shows a fibrillating baseline with no P waves and irregular, slow narrow QRS complexes at about 40 bpm: AF with a slow ventricular response, symptomatic and off rate-slowing drugs. Ventricular pacing is indicated. In haemodialysis patients, the risk of device infection is high and venous access, already used by the fistula, must be preserved. The 2021 ESC guidelines state that a leadless pacemaker should be considered when there is no upper-extremity venous access or when the risk of pocket infection is particularly high, such as after previous infection or in patients on haemodialysis. In permanent AF, VVIR is the appropriate mode.
cas-ecgc-017.aRetenir: Symptomatic slow AF in a haemodialysis patient or after infection: consider a leadless pacemaker (IIa).
cas-ecgc-017.rappel: Leadless pacemakers are implanted via the femoral vein into the right ventricle; they avoid the pocket and leads, which cause most long-term complications (infection, fracture, venous thrombosis). The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering them (class IIa) when there is no upper-extremity venous access, or when the risk of pocket infection is particularly high (previous infection, haemodialysis). Single-chamber models work in VVI(R); systems providing AV synchrony exist but remain reserved for selected indications. In permanent AF, rate-responsive ventricular pacing is the recommended mode.

cas-ecgc-018.question: Pacemaker clinic. An 81-year-old man with permanent AF had a VVI pacemaker implanted two years ago for slow AF. He becomes breathless as soon as he climbs one flight of stairs; LVEF 55%, no fluid overload. Interrogation shows 97% ventricular pacing, a rate histogram concentrated at 60 bpm, and normal thresholds and sensing. Here is the tracing recorded in clinic. What do you do?

Add an atrial lead and switch to DDD
Activate rate response (VVIR)
Lower the base rate to 50 bpm
commentaires: Incorrect: 60 bpm is the programmed rate; end of life shows as a manufacturer-defined drop in rate, and battery status is checked at interrogation.
Incorrect: in permanent AF the atrium can be neither usefully paced nor tracked.
Correct: the patient is paced continuously at a fixed rate with no acceleration on exertion: chronotropic incompetence is corrected by rate response.
Incorrect: this would reduce cardiac output on exertion even further without correcting the problem.
cas-ecgc-018.explication: The tracing shows a fibrillating baseline without P waves and regular ventricular spikes, each followed by a wide QRS: normal VVI pacing at 60 bpm, with no intrinsic QRS at all, even after exertion. The pacemaker is working properly, but the patient, whose own AV conduction is insufficient, stays at 60 bpm whatever the demand: iatrogenic chronotropic incompetence. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend rate-responsive ventricular pacing (VVIR) in permanent AF. The sensor (accelerometer, minute ventilation…) will increase the rate on exertion; the maximum sensor rate and slope should be set according to age and activity. An atrial lead makes no sense in permanent AF.
cas-ecgc-018.aRetenir: Permanent AF with 100% pacing at a fixed rate and exertional dyspnoea: activate rate response (VVIR).
cas-ecgc-018.rappel: Rate response (the fourth letter, R, of the NBG code) modulates the pacing rate according to an activity sensor (accelerometer), minute ventilation or contractility. In permanent AF, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend rate-responsive ventricular pacing (VVIR). Programming covers the maximum sensor rate, activity threshold, slope, and reaction and recovery times; it is checked with the rate histogram, a walk test or an exercise test. A histogram concentrated at the base rate in a continuously paced patient suggests chronotropic incompetence.
cas-ecgc-018.legende: Recorded after climbing two flights of stairs

cas-ecgc-019.question: Pre-MRI visit. A 79-year-old woman has an MR-conditional VVI pacemaker (complete system approved) implanted for slow AF; a lumbar MRI is planned. When the rate is temporarily programmed to 30 bpm, no intrinsic rhythm appears within 6 s and she turns pale. Here is her usual tracing. How do you program the pacemaker for the scan?
options: OVO, to remove any risk of competitive pacing
VVI unchanged, with pulse oximetry monitoring
VOO at a suitable rate, in MRI mode
VVIR, to compensate for the stress of the scan
commentaires: Incorrect: without pacing, this dependent patient would be in asystole during the scan.
Incorrect: in an inhibited mode, sensed interference can inhibit pacing in a dependent patient.
Correct: the patient is pacing-dependent: an asynchronous mode prevents pacing inhibition by MRI-induced signals.
Incorrect: rate response and advanced features must be switched off during MRI (vibration, spurious rate increases).
cas-ecgc-019.explication: The tracing shows a fibrillating baseline and regular ventricular pacing with no intrinsic QRS. The 30-bpm test confirms pacing dependence. During MRI, radiofrequency fields and gradients can be sensed as cardiac activity and inhibit pacing. The 2017 HRS consensus therefore recommends that pacing-dependent patients with an MR-conditional system be programmed to an asynchronous mode (VOO here, DOO for dual-chamber), with rate response and advanced features switched off. The rate is chosen above the intrinsic rhythm to avoid competition. The patient is monitored (ECG and pulse oximetry), with an external defibrillator and trained staff available, and the original programming is restored afterwards.
cas-ecgc-019.aRetenir: MRI in a pacing-dependent patient: asynchronous mode (VOO/DOO), rate response off, continuous monitoring.
cas-ecgc-019.rappel: Before MRI, it must be checked that the whole system (generator and leads) is MR conditional according to the manufacturer's conditions, and pacing dependence must be assessed. According to the 2017 HRS consensus, pacing-dependent patients are programmed to an asynchronous mode (DOO/VOO) with rate response and advanced features switched off; non-dependent patients may be programmed to a non-pacing (ODO/OVO) or inhibited (DDI/VVI) mode. Monitoring includes at least ECG and pulse oximetry, with a defibrillator and staff trained in resuscitation. The original programming is restored and the system checked at the end of the scan.

cas-ecgc-020.question: Day-1 check after implantation. A 70-year-old woman had a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted for symptomatic sick sinus syndrome; before implantation her PR was 160 ms with narrow QRS complexes. The device is in DDD 60 bpm with nominal settings. Here is her resting ECG. Which setting do you change?

Shorten the AV delay to 120 ms to secure capture
Program VVI 40 so that pacing is backup only
None, 100% AV pacing is the goal
commentaires: Correct: AV conduction is normal: permanent ventricular pacing is unnecessary and harmful; intrinsic conduction should be promoted.
Incorrect: this would force even more ventricular pacing with no benefit for this patient.
Incorrect: sinus node dysfunction would no longer be treated, and the atrium would be neither paced nor tracked.
Incorrect: the goal in sinus node dysfunction is to pace the atrium and let the ventricle conduct.
cas-ecgc-020.explication: Each cycle comprises an atrial spike followed by a P wave, then a second spike followed by a wide QRS: AV sequential pacing at 60 bpm. The nominal AV delay (here 180 ms, measured between the two spikes) is shorter than the patient's own conduction time after atrial pacing, which is longer than her spontaneous PR of 160 ms: the ventricle is therefore paced on every cycle despite normal conduction. This unnecessary ventricular pacing desynchronises the left ventricle and increases the risk of AF and heart failure. cas-ecgc-020.aRetenir: Sinus node dysfunction with normal AV conduction: do not let a DDD device pace the ventricle unnecessarily.
cas-ecgc-020.rappel: After atrial pacing, AV conduction time (AP–VS) is longer than the spontaneous PR (AS–VS) by about 30 to 60 ms, owing to capture latency and intra-atrial conduction from the lead. A nominal AV delay of 150 to 200 ms therefore often results in permanent ventricular pacing even when conduction is normal. Two families of algorithms limit this pacing: AAI(R)–DDD(R) mode switching, which tolerates isolated non-conducted P waves, and AV hysteresis or AV search, which periodically lengthens the AV delay. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend minimising unnecessary ventricular pacing in patients with DDD pacemakers for sinus node dysfunction.

cas-ecgc-021.question: Heart failure clinic. A 74-year-old man had a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted six years ago for complete AV block; LVEF was 60% before implantation. He has had NYHA class III dyspnoea for a year, with LVEF now 32% despite optimal medical therapy and normal coronary angiography. Interrogation shows 99% ventricular pacing. Here is the ECG. What is the most appropriate proposal?

Program VVI 40 to reduce pacing
Replace it with a single-chamber ICD
Upgrade to cardiac resynchronisation therapy
commentaires: Incorrect: the patient has complete AV block; no lengthening of the AV delay will bring out intrinsic conduction.
Incorrect: this would merely slow down a patient with complete block without eliminating RV pacing.
Incorrect: this would retain 99% RV pacing, which is the cause of the ventricular dysfunction.
Correct: RV pacing-induced cardiomyopathy with LVEF ≤ 35% despite therapy: an upgrade to CRT (or conduction system pacing) should be considered.
cas-ecgc-021.explication: The ECG shows sequential atrial then ventricular pacing on every cycle, with wide QRS complexes of RV origin. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering (class IIa) an upgrade to CRT in paced patients who develop heart failure with LVEF ≤ 35% despite optimal therapy and a significant proportion of RV pacing. cas-ecgc-021.aRetenir: Near-permanent RV pacing and a collapsed LVEF: pacing-induced cardiomyopathy; consider CRT or conduction system pacing.
cas-ecgc-021.rappel: Pacing-induced cardiomyopathy is usually defined as a fall in LVEF of at least 10 points to an LVEF < 50% in a patient with RV pacing, in the absence of another cause; the risk increases above 20% RV pacing. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering (class IIa) an upgrade to CRT in paced patients who develop symptomatic heart failure with LVEF ≤ 35% despite optimal therapy and a significant proportion of RV pacing. In patients with LVEF < 40% who are expected to need substantial pacing for AV block, CRT is preferred over RV pacing from the outset. The 2023 HRS guideline regards conduction system pacing as a reasonable alternative.

cas-ecgc-022.question: Call from the anaesthetist the day before a colectomy by laparotomy. A 77-year-old man has a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted for complete AV block; at the last check no escape rhythm appeared at 30 bpm. The surgeon will use monopolar diathermy. Here is the preoperative ECG. What is the recommended management?
options: Switch pacing off during surgery
Program an asynchronous mode (DOO) before surgery
No precautions: the device filters these signals
Activate rate response to prevent bradycardia
commentaires: Incorrect: in a patient with no escape rhythm, switching pacing off would cause asystole.
Correct: a pacing-dependent patient and monopolar diathermy above the iliac crest: asynchronous pacing prevents interference from inhibiting pacing.
Incorrect: diathermy signals can be sensed and inhibit pacing, which is dangerous in a dependent patient.
Incorrect: rate response provides no protection against inhibition and should actually be switched off in theatre.
cas-ecgc-022.explication: The ECG shows AV sequential pacing on every cycle, consistent with paced complete AV block. The patient is pacing-dependent, since no intrinsic rhythm appears at 30 bpm. During abdominal surgery above the iliac crest with monopolar diathermy, electromagnetic interference can be sensed and inhibit pacing. In dependent patients, the 2022 EHRA consensus advises asynchronous pacing (DOO or VOO) at a rate above the intrinsic rhythm: by magnet, preferred when the generator remains accessible and its magnet response has been checked, or by reprogramming, which is needed if the operative field is less than 15 cm from the generator or if a magnet cannot be kept in place. Bipolar or ultrasonic instruments and short bursts should also be preferred, the return electrode placed as far as possible from the generator, ECG and pulse monitored, and the pacemaker checked after surgery. Switching pacing off would cause asystole, and rate response offers no protection.
cas-ecgc-022.aRetenir: Pacing-dependent patient and monopolar diathermy above the iliac crest: asynchronous pacing (magnet or reprogramming) and a postoperative check.
cas-ecgc-022.rappel: Monopolar diathermy generates electromagnetic interference, which is more likely the closer the operative field is to the generator; according to the 2022 EHRA consensus, the risk is very low for surgery below the iliac crest with the return electrode on the thigh. In pacemaker patients the main risk is inhibition due to oversensing, which is serious in dependent patients. The consensus recommends asynchronous pacing for these patients, by magnet if the generator is accessible, or by reprogramming if the operative field is less than 15 cm from the generator or if a magnet cannot be kept in place. For all device patients: ECG and pulse monitoring, bipolar or ultrasonic instruments where possible, short bursts, a return electrode away from the generator and no full-body return electrode. The device is checked after surgery if its programming was changed or if the procedure carried a high risk of interference.

cas-ecgc-023.question: Arrhythmia clinic. A 34-year-old woman with congenital complete AV block has a DDD pacemaker. A runner, she experiences sudden fatigue beyond a certain level of effort, "as if the heart halved its speed". Settings: maximum tracking rate 130 bpm, sensed AV delay 150 ms, PVARP 300 ms. Here is her tracing during warm-up. Which reprogramming do you propose?

Shorten the PVARP and raise the maximum tracking rate
Program DDIR with aggressive rate response
Enable mode switching whenever the atrial rate exceeds 130 bpm
commentaires: Incorrect: lengthening the AV delay lengthens the total atrial refractory period and further lowers the 2:1 block rate.
Correct: the total atrial refractory period (150 + 300 = 450 ms) imposes 2:1 block at about 133 bpm; it must be shortened and the maximum tracking rate raised.
Incorrect: DDIR no longer tracks the atrium; in a patient with a normal sinus node, physiological AV synchrony during exercise would be lost.
Incorrect: mode switching is designed for atrial arrhythmias; applied to exercise sinus tachycardia, it would abolish atrial tracking.
cas-ecgc-023.explication: The tracing shows sinus P waves, each followed by a ventricular spike after a constant delay and then a wide QRS: normal atrial tracking (VDD-type operation) at 95 bpm. The problem occurs at higher rates. The total atrial refractory period (TARP = AV delay + PVARP) is 150 + 300 = 450 ms: any P wave occurring at an interval shorter than 450 ms, i.e. above about 133 bpm, falls into the PVARP every other beat and is not tracked. The ventricular rate then abruptly halves (electronic 2:1 block), which explains the sensation described. In a young athlete, the TARP should be shortened (shorter PVARP, dynamic AV delay that shortens with rate) and the maximum tracking rate raised, while keeping the 2:1 block rate above it.
cas-ecgc-023.aRetenir: Exercise-induced 2:1 block in a DDD patient: the TARP (AV delay + PVARP) sets the 2:1 rate; shorten it and raise the MTR.
cas-ecgc-023.rappel: In DDD mode, the total atrial refractory period (TARP) is the sum of the AV delay and the PVARP; the 2:1 block rate equals 60,000 / TARP (in ms). Between the maximum tracking rate (MTR) and the 2:1 block rate, the pacemaker shows pseudo-Wenckebach behaviour, which is gradual and well tolerated. If the 2:1 rate is close to or below the MTR, the switch to 2:1 is abrupt. In young active patients, a high MTR, a short PVARP (with post-PVC extension to prevent PMT) and a dynamic AV delay are programmed so that the 2:1 block rate stays well above the MTR.

cas-ecgc-024.question: Device clinic. A 68-year-old man has a dual-chamber pacemaker implanted for sinus node dysfunction, programmed with an AAI(R)–DDD(R) switching algorithm. The resident is concerned: "the ventricle is never paced even though there is an RV lead; we should shorten the AV delay". Here is the tracing. What do you tell him?

Ventricular undersensing: increase the sensitivity
Dislodged RV lead: urgent chest X-ray
Expected function: change nothing
commentaires: Incorrect: no ventricular spike is delivered, so there can be no loss of ventricular capture.
Incorrect: ventricular undersensing would produce inappropriate V spikes, which are absent here.
Incorrect: the absence of ventricular pacing is intended; nothing suggests lead dislodgement.
Correct: atrial pacing followed by intrinsic AV conduction with narrow QRS: exactly what the algorithm minimising ventricular pacing is designed to achieve.
cas-ecgc-024.explication: Each cycle begins with a spike followed by a P wave (atrial capture), then a narrow QRS conducted after about 200 ms: atrial pacing with intrinsic AV conduction. cas-ecgc-024.rappel: AAI(R)–DDD(R) switching algorithms (for example Medtronic MVP, MicroPort SafeR or equivalents) operate in an atrial mode with ventricular monitoring and switch to DDD after loss of conduction over a defined number of cycles. They therefore tolerate isolated non-conducted P waves and long PR intervals. The SAVE PACe trial showed that a strategy minimising ventricular pacing reduced the risk of persistent AF in sinus node dysfunction. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend minimising unnecessary ventricular pacing in these patients; a very long PR (> 300 ms) under such an algorithm should nevertheless be monitored, as it can become symptomatic.

cas-ecgc-025.question: Three-month check after cardiac resynchronisation. A 69-year-old woman with dilated cardiomyopathy had left bundle branch block of 170 ms before implantation; she feels better. The ward nurse recorded this rhythm strip and asks whether LV pacing is effective. What is the most relevant approach?

Conclude that the LV is captured because the paced QRS is narrow
Perform an urgent dyssynchrony echocardiogram
Program LV-only pacing to check its effect
commentaires: Correct: LV capture is assessed on the 12-lead ECG: a dominant R wave in V1 and a negative pattern in lead I, without return to the LBBB pattern.
Incorrect: a single lead is not enough; a relatively narrow QRS may also result from fusion with intrinsic conduction.
Incorrect: echocardiography is not the tool for checking LV capture; the ECG and interrogation are sufficient.
Incorrect: changing the pacing mode for a simple check is not the approach; the LV threshold is tested at interrogation if needed.
cas-ecgc-025.explication: The tracing shows sinus P waves followed, after a short delay, by a spike and a relatively narrow paced QRS: biventricular pacing with atrial tracking. A single lead cannot confirm LV capture: RV-only pacing would also give a paced QRS, and fusion with intrinsic conduction can narrow the QRS. Verification relies on the 12-lead ECG: with effective biventricular pacing, a dominant R wave (or a qR/Rs pattern) in V1 and a negative pattern (Q, qR or QS) in lead I are expected. cas-ecgc-025.aRetenir: LV capture in CRT is judged on the 12-lead ECG (R wave in V1, negative lead I), never on a single rhythm strip.
cas-ecgc-025.rappel: With RV apical pacing, the QRS has a left bundle branch block-like pattern (QS in V1) with left axis deviation. With effective biventricular pacing, activation also starts from the LV lateral wall: a dominant R wave in V1 in most cases and a negative lead I. Loss of LV capture returns the pattern to that of isolated RV pacing. A paced QRS narrower than the intrinsic QRS is desirable but does not prove capture. It must also be checked that the percentage of effective biventricular pacing remains ≥ 98%.

cas-ecgc-026.question: Cardiology ward, the day after implantation of a VVI pacemaker (passive-fixation lead) in an 88-year-old woman with complete AV block and limited mobility (VVI chosen because of her age). The monitor alarm sounds just after she gets up for the first time; she is pale and nauseated. Here is the tracing. What is the most appropriate management?

Place a magnet over the generator
Increase output, chest X-ray, lead revision
Observe: a maturation phenomenon that resolves within a month
commentaires: Incorrect: the problem is not sensing; the spikes are delivered at the right time but fail to capture.
Incorrect: a magnet suspends sensing but does not improve capture; it does not correct ineffective spikes.
Correct: intermittent loss of ventricular capture the day after implantation: lead dislodgement until proven otherwise; secure pacing, confirm, then reposition.
Incorrect: in a dependent, symptomatic patient waiting is not an option; maturation threshold rise does not explain overt loss of capture on day 1.
cas-ecgc-026.explication: The ventricular spikes are delivered regularly; most are followed by a wide QRS, but three are not, and no escape rhythm fills the gap: intermittent loss of ventricular capture in a dependent patient. In the background, sinus P waves are dissociated (complete AV block). A magnet does not improve capture.
cas-ecgc-026.aRetenir: Loss of capture in the days after implantation: lead dislodgement until proven otherwise; secure pacing, confirm, reposition.
cas-ecgc-026.rappel: Loss of capture is recognised by a spike delivered at the expected time but not followed by depolarisation. Its causes depend on timing: lead dislodgement or perforation in the first days or weeks, threshold rise (inflammation, fibrosis, exit block), metabolic disturbances (hyperkalaemia, acidosis), drugs (class IC antiarrhythmics), conductor or insulation failure, or inadequate programmed output. The usual safety margin is twice the threshold in amplitude or three times in pulse width. In a dependent patient, output is increased urgently before the cause is sought.

cas-ecgc-027.question: Dialysis unit. A 67-year-old man on haemodialysis has a VVI pacemaker for complete AV block; he missed his session two days ago. He complains of weakness, BP 95/60 mmHg; potassium 7.6 mmol/L. The ventricular threshold was 0.75 V at the last check, with output programmed at 2.5 V. Here is the monitor strip. Which measures are appropriate? (select all that apply)

Temporarily increase pulse amplitude and pulse width
Arrange an urgent lead replacement

Incorrect: this is loss of capture, not a sensing problem.
Correct: until the metabolic disturbance is corrected, increasing output can restore capture in this dependent patient.
Incorrect: the lead is probably intact; the cause is metabolic and reversible.
cas-ecgc-027.explication: The tracing shows regular ventricular spikes, three of which are followed by no QRS and no escape, on a background of dissociated P waves: loss of ventricular capture in a dependent patient.
