The lead is not at fault and sensitivity is irrelevant; the threshold is rechecked after correction.
cas-ecgc-027.aRetenir: Loss of capture in a dialysis patient: think hyperkalaemia; calcium, lowering potassium and a temporary increase in output.
cas-ecgc-027.rappel: Hyperkalaemia reduces the resting membrane potential and myocardial excitability: it raises pacing thresholds, especially above 7 mmol/L, and can cause loss of capture, capture latency and widening of paced QRS complexes. It can also reduce signal amplitude and impair sensing. Treatment relies on IV calcium, insulin–glucose, β2-agonists and removal (dialysis). Thresholds normalise after correction; in dependent patients output is increased in the meantime.

cas-ecgc-028.question: Cardioversion room. A 75-year-old man has a VVI pacemaker for complete AV block; a 200 J external shock (anterolateral pads, the anterior pad 5 cm from the generator) has just terminated persistent AF. He is conscious, but the rhythm has changed. Here is the monitor strip. What is the immediate management?
options: Deliver a second shock to "resynchronise" the device
Program a more sensitive ventricular setting
Increase ventricular output, then interrogate and test the threshold
Give amiodarone to stabilise sinus rhythm
commentaires: Incorrect: another shock would further injure the electrode–myocardium interface with no benefit.
Incorrect: the spikes are delivered at the right time; they fail to capture, which is not a sensing problem.
Correct: the shock transiently raised the threshold at the lead–tissue interface; increase output, measure the threshold and check the system.
Incorrect: amiodarone can raise thresholds further and does not address the loss of capture.
cas-ecgc-028.explication: After cardioversion, sinus P waves are visible and dissociated (complete AV block), while several ventricular spikes are followed by no QRS: intermittent loss of ventricular capture without escape. Shock current can travel along the lead and injure the electrode–myocardium interface, transiently raising the threshold; more rarely it causes an electrical reset of the device. The risk is greater the closer the pad is to the generator. Output must be increased immediately (or transcutaneous pacing used), the device interrogated and threshold and impedance measured, then the patient monitored until normalisation. The 2022 EHRA consensus recommends an anteroposterior pad position where possible, with the anterior pad as far as possible from the generator (at least 15 cm), and interrogation of the device after cardioversion.
cas-ecgc-028.aRetenir: Loss of capture after cardioversion: transient threshold rise; increase output, interrogate, and in future place the pads well away from the generator (≥ 15 cm).
cas-ecgc-028.rappel: An external shock in a pacemaker patient can cause a transient rise in pacing thresholds, an electrical reset (backup mode) or, exceptionally, circuit failure. The 2022 EHRA consensus recommends an anteroposterior pad position with the anterior pad at least 15 cm from the generator, choosing energy and pad position to minimise current flow through the generator and leads, having external pacing available for dependent patients, and interrogating the device after cardioversion or before discharge. Programming output with an adequate safety margin limits the consequences of a threshold rise.

cas-ecgc-029.question: Arrhythmia clinic. A 71-year-old woman with sick sinus syndrome and paroxysmal AF has a pacemaker programmed to AAIR (normal AV conduction, atrial threshold 1.0 V at the last check, output 2.0 V). Flecainide was increased from 100 to 200 mg/day ten days ago; since then she has noticed "gaps" and dizziness. Here is the tracing. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Rise in atrial threshold on flecainide
Flecainide-induced paroxysmal AV block
Atrial oversensing of myopotentials
Slow atrial flutter organised by flecainide
commentaires: Correct: class IC antiarrhythmic drugs raise pacing thresholds; with a narrow margin, atrial capture becomes intermittent.
Incorrect: AV block would appear as a paced P wave not followed by a QRS; here it is the P wave itself that is missing after the spike.
Incorrect: oversensing would inhibit spike delivery; here the spikes are delivered on time.
Incorrect: no rapid organised atrial activity is visible; cycles are regular apart from the ineffective spikes.
cas-ecgc-029.explication: Most spikes are followed by a P wave and then a narrow conducted QRS; two spikes are followed by neither a P wave nor a QRS, creating a pause: intermittent loss of atrial capture, with no ventricular backup since the mode is AAI. Class IC antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone), through their effect on the sodium current, raise pacing thresholds in a dose-dependent way. With an output of 2.0 V for an initial threshold of 1.0 V, the safety margin is small. Management is to measure the atrial threshold, increase output with an adequate margin and reassess the dose; switching to a dual-chamber mode with ventricular pacing minimisation would also provide ventricular protection.
cas-ecgc-029.aRetenir: Loss of capture after increasing a class IC antiarrhythmic: think threshold rise and check the safety margin.
cas-ecgc-029.rappel: Several drugs raise pacing thresholds: mainly class IC antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone), and to a lesser extent amiodarone and high-dose sotalol. Metabolic disturbances (hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypoxia) have the same effect. After starting or increasing such a drug in a pacemaker patient, it is prudent to check the threshold and maintain a safety margin of at least twice the threshold in amplitude. In AAI mode, loss of atrial capture causes a pause with no ventricular backup.

cas-ecgc-030.question: Endoscopy suite. An 82-year-old man has a single-chamber ventricular pacemaker implanted for slow AF and has returned to sinus rhythm on amiodarone. For a polypectomy with a diathermy snare, the anaesthetist has placed a magnet over the generator. The nurse calls because "the pacemaker has gone haywire". Here is the monitor strip. What do you reply?
options: Loss of capture: remove the magnet and increase amplitude
Battery depletion: urgent generator replacement
Ventricular tachycardia: prepare the defibrillator
Expected magnet response: asynchronous pacing
commentaires: Incorrect: the spikes not followed by a QRS fall in the ventricular refractory period just after an intrinsic QRS; this is not loss of capture.
Incorrect: the magnet rate reflects battery status, but the competition with the sinus rhythm here is simply due to the magnet.
Incorrect: the wide QRS complexes are preceded by a spike and interspersed with narrow sinus QRS complexes; there is no VT.
Correct: under a magnet the pacemaker paces at a fixed rate without sensing; competition with sinus rhythm is expected and transient.
cas-ecgc-030.explication: Sinus rhythm at about 78 bpm coexists with regular, slightly faster ventricular spikes delivered regardless of the intrinsic QRS complexes: some capture (wide QRS), others fall just after an intrinsic QRS, in the refractory period, and have no effect. This is asynchronous pacing (VOO). In a pacemaker, a magnet suspends sensing and imposes asynchronous pacing at the magnet rate, which is specific to each manufacturer and to battery status. This behaviour is intended here to protect against diathermy interference. Competition with sinus rhythm is usually harmless. When the magnet is removed, programmed function resumes automatically.
cas-ecgc-030.aRetenir: Magnet on a pacemaker = asynchronous pacing at the magnet rate; competition with the intrinsic rhythm is expected.
cas-ecgc-030.rappel: On a pacemaker, applying a magnet switches the device to an asynchronous mode (VOO, AOO or DOO) at a manufacturer-specific magnet rate, 85 to 100 bpm at beginning of life according to the 2022 EHRA consensus, which decreases as the battery approaches end of life. The response is not universal: some devices can be programmed not to respond to a magnet, some Biotronik pacemakers in "AUTO" mode pace asynchronously for only 10 beats, and the Micra leadless pacemaker has no magnet response. Removing the magnet restores programmed function. On an ICD, by contrast, a magnet suspends tachyarrhythmia detection or therapies without changing bradycardia pacing.

cas-ecgc-031.question: Cardiac intensive care unit, day 2 after a large revascularised anterior myocardial infarction. A 70-year-old man has a VVI 60 bpm pacemaker implanted last year for slow AF and is now in sinus rhythm. Interrogation shows the intrinsic R wave has fallen from 9 to 2 mV, programmed sensitivity 2.5 mV and a stable capture threshold. Here is the monitor strip. Which programming corrects the problem?
options: Set the sensitivity to 4 mV to filter out noise
Program a more sensitive setting, about 0.9 mV
Increase pacing amplitude to 5 V
Program VOO to avoid pauses
commentaires: Incorrect: raising the mV value would make the device even less sensitive and worsen undersensing.
Correct: the R wave (2 mV) is smaller than the programmed sensitivity value (2.5 mV); the mV value must be lowered to sense it with a margin of about twofold.
Incorrect: capture is preserved; pacing amplitude does not affect sensing.
Incorrect: VOO would make asynchronous pacing permanent, which is exactly the problem observed.
cas-ecgc-031.explication: Conducted sinus rhythm at about 78 bpm coexists with ventricular spikes delivered at fixed intervals (60 bpm) regardless of the intrinsic QRS complexes: some capture, others fall in the refractory period. The pacemaker does not "see" the QRS complexes: ventricular undersensing. The infarct has reduced the amplitude of the local signal, which is now below the programmed sensitivity value. The pacemaker must be made more sensitive, i.e. the millivolt value lowered (to about half the R-wave amplitude), and oversensing then excluded. A spike falling on the T wave rarely triggers a ventricular arrhythmia, hence the value of prompt correction in this ischaemic setting.
cas-ecgc-031.aRetenir: Undersensing: make the device more sensitive by lowering the mV value (about half the R-wave amplitude).
cas-ecgc-031.rappel: Sensitivity is the amplitude threshold above which a signal is sensed: the lower the mV value, the more sensitive the device. A margin of about twofold is recommended (sensitivity ≤ half the measured amplitude). Causes of undersensing include reduced signal amplitude (infarction, fibrosis, cardiomyopathy, lead dislodgement), metabolic disturbances, lead failure, inappropriate programming, or a signal falling in a refractory or blanking period. Undersensing leads to competitive pacing, which is rarely arrhythmogenic.

cas-ecgc-032.question: Operating theatre, left total shoulder replacement. An 80-year-old woman has a left pectoral VVI pacemaker for complete AV block with no known escape rhythm; the pacemaker was not reprogrammed. The surgeon is using monopolar diathermy; the anaesthetist reports a drop in blood pressure with each application. Here is the monitor strip. What is the immediate management?
options: Give atropine with each application
Apply a magnet and limit diathermy bursts
Increase pacing amplitude
Carry on: the device will switch to noise mode by itself
commentaires: Incorrect: atropine has no effect on complete AV block without escape or on pacemaker inhibition.
Correct: oversensing of interference with inhibition in a dependent patient: a magnet imposes asynchronous pacing, and short bursts limit inhibition.
Incorrect: there is no spike during the pause; this is not a capture failure but inhibition.
Incorrect: noise reversion is not reliable for all types of interference, and the pause is already symptomatic.
cas-ecgc-032.explication: The P waves are dissociated from regular paced QRS complexes (complete AV block paced in VVI); during a period when the baseline is noisy, no spike is delivered and no QRS appears for almost 3 s. The pacemaker interprets the noise as ventricular activity and inhibits itself: oversensing of electromagnetic interference due to monopolar diathermy used close to the generator. In this dependent patient, a magnet must immediately be placed over the generator (asynchronous pacing) and the surgeon asked to use short bursts, ideally with bipolar diathermy. As the operative field is less than 15 cm from the generator, the 2022 EHRA consensus called for preoperative reprogramming to an asynchronous mode, since a magnet is hard to keep in place so close to the field; if a magnet cannot be applied, diathermy must be suspended until the device is reprogrammed. The pacemaker will be checked after surgery.
cas-ecgc-032.aRetenir: Pause without spikes during diathermy in a pacing-dependent patient: inhibition by interference; immediate magnet and short bursts.
cas-ecgc-032.rappel: Electromagnetic interference can be sensed as cardiac activity: in an inhibited mode it suspends pacing; in DDD, spurious atrial sensing can trigger rapid ventricular pacing. Pacemakers have noise reversion (asynchronous pacing if noise is continuous within a dedicated window), but it is not reliable for all interference. For dependent patients exposed to monopolar diathermy close to the generator, the 2022 EHRA consensus recommends asynchronous pacing: a magnet if the generator is accessible, reprogramming if the operative field is less than 15 cm from the generator. Any pause due to oversensing in a dependent patient is an emergency.

cas-ecgc-033.question: Holter review. A 76-year-old man has a VVI pacemaker implanted nine years ago for complete AV block (lead in unipolar configuration) and is referred for brief spells while doing DIY. Here is the strip coinciding with a spell. Which mechanisms can explain this abnormality? (select all that apply)
options: Programmed rate hysteresis
Oversensing of pectoral myopotentials
Generator battery depletion
Partial conductor fracture of the lead
Loss of ventricular capture
commentaires: Incorrect: hysteresis lengthens the escape interval only after a sensed QRS, and never by nearly 3 s.
Correct: with unipolar sensing, pectoral muscle activity is picked up between the tip electrode and the can and inhibits pacing.
Incorrect: battery depletion gradually lowers the pacing rate but does not create an isolated pause with noise.
Correct: a fracture produces intermittent make-break signals sensed as QRS complexes, causing inhibition.
Incorrect: loss of capture would leave visible spikes not followed by QRS complexes; here no spike is delivered during the pause.
cas-ecgc-033.explication: The tracing shows regular paced QRS complexes dissociated from the P waves (complete AV block), then a pause of about 3 s without any spike, during which the baseline is contaminated by high-frequency activity, before pacing resumes. The absence of spikes signals inhibition, hence oversensing. In unipolar configuration, during upper-limb exertion, pectoral myopotentials are a classic cause; conductor fracture, plausible in a nine-year-old lead, produces intermittent signals with the same effect. They are distinguished at interrogation (impedance, electrograms, provocative manoeuvres). Loss of capture would leave visible spikes; hysteresis and battery depletion do not produce a noisy pause of this kind.
cas-ecgc-033.aRetenir: A pause without spikes in a paced patient = oversensing (myopotentials, fracture, interference) until proven otherwise.
cas-ecgc-033.rappel: When a pacemaker patient has a pause, the presence or absence of a spike is the key: a spike not followed by depolarisation indicates loss of capture; the absence of a spike beyond the escape interval indicates oversensing (or, more rarely, output failure). Oversensed signals may be physiological (myopotentials, T waves, far-field P waves) or non-physiological (fracture, insulation breach, loose connection, external interference). Programming bipolar sensing or a less sensitive setting corrects myopotential oversensing; a fracture requires lead replacement.

cas-ecgc-034.question: Pacemaker clinic. A 73-year-old man has a dual-chamber pacemaker for sick sinus syndrome, spontaneous PR 200 ms, sensed AV delay programmed at 170 ms. The technician shows you this tracing: "some spikes fall within the QRS without changing it, surely we have loss of capture; shall I increase the amplitude?". What do you decide?
options: Increase amplitude to 5 V to restore capture
Program a more sensitive ventricular setting
Shorten the AV delay to 120 ms
Keep amplitude, lengthen the AV delay
commentaires: Incorrect: the spike falls within a QRS already under way, in the refractory period; more energy would change nothing and drain the battery.
Incorrect: the QRS is not yet detectable at the RV lead when the AV delay expires; this is not a sensitivity problem.
Incorrect: this would abolish fusion at the cost of permanent ventricular pacing, which is unnecessary in this patient.
Correct: these are pseudofusion beats caused by an AV delay close to the spontaneous PR; intrinsic conduction should be promoted, not output increased.
cas-ecgc-034.explication: Each sinus P wave is followed by a wide paced QRS, a narrow intrinsic QRS, an intermediate complex preceded by a spike (fusion), or an unchanged intrinsic QRS containing a spike (pseudofusion). The AV delay (170 ms) is close to the spontaneous PR (200 ms): the ventricular spike is delivered when spontaneous depolarisation has already begun but has not yet reached the RV lead. In pseudofusion, the spike falls on myocardium that is already depolarising and has no effect: this is not loss of capture. In a patient implanted for sinus node dysfunction, the right response is to promote intrinsic conduction (longer AV delay, hysteresis or an algorithm minimising ventricular pacing).
cas-ecgc-034.aRetenir: A spike within an unchanged intrinsic QRS = pseudofusion, not loss of capture; adjust the AV delay, not the amplitude.
cas-ecgc-034.rappel: Fusion is ventricular depolarisation caused partly by the stimulus and partly by spontaneous activation: the QRS has an intermediate morphology. Pseudofusion is a spike delivered within an intrinsic QRS that it does not alter, because the myocardium near the electrode is already depolarised. These phenomena occur when the AV delay or escape interval is close to the spontaneous conduction time; they are physiological and require no change in output. To diagnose loss of capture, the spike must fall outside the refractory period and not be followed by depolarisation.

cas-ecgc-035.question: Holter review. A 79-year-old woman has a dual-chamber pacemaker for paroxysmal AV block. Settings: lower rate 70 bpm, maximum tracking rate 110 bpm, maximum sensor rate 130 bpm, PVARP 250 ms. She reports palpitations on going to bed. Here is the corresponding strip. What is the interpretation?
options: PMT triggered by a PVC
Sinus tachycardia tracked by the pacemaker
Rate increase driven by rate response
Slow ventricular tachycardia
commentaires: Correct: PVC, a retrograde P wave followed by ventricular pacing, rate locked at the maximum tracking rate: a PMT loop.
Incorrect: the tachycardia starts abruptly after a PVC, and the atrial wave is retrograde, negative in lead II, at a fixed interval after each paced QRS.
Incorrect: the patient is going to bed, and rate response could reach 130 bpm; a rate locked at 110 bpm corresponds to atrial tracking.
Incorrect: every QRS is preceded by a spike; these are paced QRS complexes, not VT.
cas-ecgc-035.explication: The tracing begins with two cycles of AV sequential pacing at 70 bpm, then a PVC occurs. It is followed by a retrograde P wave (negative in lead II), which is sensed and tracked by ventricular pacing; each paced QRS is again conducted retrogradely to the atrium, and the loop is sustained. The rate is fixed at 110 bpm, exactly the maximum tracking rate, because the retrograde VA interval plus the AV delay is shorter than the MTR cycle: this is pacemaker-mediated tachycardia. Initiation by a PVC, a rate capped at the MTR and a retrograde P wave are characteristic. Rate response is capped at 130 bpm and would not explain acceleration on going to bed.
cas-ecgc-035.aRetenir: Paced tachycardia at the MTR, triggered by a PVC with a retrograde P wave: PMT.
cas-ecgc-035.rappel: PMT is a loop tachycardia: the pacemaker forms the antegrade limb (tracking the sensed P wave) and the patient's retrograde VA conduction the retrograde limb. It is typically triggered by a PVC, loss of atrial capture or an untracked P wave, which dissociate atrium and ventricle. It occurs at or just below the maximum tracking rate. It requires preserved VA conduction and a retrograde P wave falling outside the PVARP. It is terminated by a magnet (asynchronous mode) or by the device's dedicated algorithm; it is prevented by a PVARP longer than VA conduction, PVARP extension after a PVC or a PMT algorithm.
cas-ecgc-035.legende: Holter, 11:40 pm: "palpitations on going to bed"

cas-ecgc-036.question: Arrhythmia clinic. A 70-year-old man has a dual-chamber pacemaker for complete AV block. Two weeks ago he attended the emergency department with palpitations; this tracing was recorded there and the episode was terminated with a magnet. Settings: maximum tracking rate 120 bpm, sensed AV delay 150 ms, PVARP 250 ms, with no post-PVC extension. The retrograde conduction test measures a VP–retrograde P interval of 330 ms. Which programming best prevents recurrence while preserving atrial tracking on exertion?
options: Set a permanent fixed PVARP of 450 ms at all rates
Lower the maximum tracking rate to 100 bpm
Enable post-PVC PVARP extension and the PMT algorithm
Program a less sensitive atrial setting
commentaires: Incorrect: this PVARP covers VA conduction, but with a 150 ms AV delay it imposes 2:1 block from 100 bpm, below the maximum tracking rate.
Incorrect: the PMT would simply be slower; the loop would persist and exercise capacity would be limited.
Correct: the PVARP is extended only after a PVC, the cycle on which the loop starts, and the algorithm breaks an established loop: tracking on exertion is preserved.
Incorrect: this would risk undersensing sinus P waves, with no guarantee that the retrograde wave would no longer be sensed.
cas-ecgc-036.explication: The tracing shows the typical onset: two AP–VP cycles, a PVC, a retrograde P wave sensed outside the PVARP, then ventricular pacing at 120 bpm, the maximum tracking rate, sustained by VA conduction. The measured VP–retrograde P interval (330 ms) exceeds the programmed PVARP (250 ms), which explains why the retrograde wave is tracked. Lengthening the fixed PVARP beyond 330 ms (with a margin, about 400 to 450 ms) would prevent the loop, but the total atrial refractory period (AV delay + PVARP ≈ 600 ms) would limit atrial tracking to about 100 bpm, below the MTR. The best option is targeted: automatic PVARP extension after a PVC (the main trigger) and a PMT detection and termination algorithm, which briefly lengthens the PVARP when sustained pacing at the MTR is recognised.
cas-ecgc-036.aRetenir: Preventing PMT: post-PVC PVARP extension and a PMT algorithm rather than a long fixed PVARP that limits exercise tracking.
cas-ecgc-036.rappel: For PMT to occur, the retrograde P wave must fall outside the PVARP. A fixed PVARP longer than VA conduction prevents it, but lengthens the total atrial refractory period (AV delay + PVARP) and lowers the 2:1 block rate (60,000 / TARP). Devices therefore offer PVARP extension (often to 400 ms or more) on the single cycle after a PVC, and algorithms that recognise sustained pacing at the MTR with a stable VP–AS interval and then extend the PVARP or withhold one ventricular pace to break the loop. VA conduction is measured at the programmer with a retrograde conduction test.

cas-ecgc-037.question: Overnight telemetry. A 45-year-old man admitted with pneumonia, asymptomatic and on no rate-slowing drugs; the conducted beats have a PR of 200 ms and narrow QRS complexes. Statement: this tracing alone does not show whether the block is nodal or infranodal.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: in 2:1 AV block, two consecutive PR intervals are never seen; neither QRS width nor the PR is enough to prove the level.
Incorrect: a narrow QRS makes nodal block more likely, particularly at night in a young person, but intra-His block remains possible; the level must be clarified by other findings.
cas-ecgc-037.explication: Every other P wave is conducted, with a constant PR and narrow QRS complexes: 2:1 AV block. This rhythm cannot be classified as Mobitz I or Mobitz II, since no progressive PR prolongation can be observed. The narrow QRS, nocturnal occurrence and background (young patient, fever, possible high vagal tone) point to functional nodal block, but narrow-QRS intra-His block does exist. Localisation relies on other findings: Wenckebach periods elsewhere on the recording, response to exercise or atropine and, if doubt persists, an EP study.
cas-ecgc-037.aRetenir: 2:1 AV block: the level cannot be read from a single tracing; look for Wenckebach periods and test the response to exercise.
cas-ecgc-037.rappel: In 2:1 AV block, alternating conduction prevents analysis of PR behaviour. Features favouring a nodal level: narrow QRS, long PR in conducted beats, Wenckebach periods on the same recording, nocturnal or vagal occurrence, improvement with exercise or atropine. Features favouring an infranodal level: wide QRS, normal PR, worsening on exercise, improvement with carotid sinus massage. Isolated nocturnal narrow-QRS 2:1 AV block in a young asymptomatic person usually calls for observation only.

cas-ecgc-038.question: Cardiac intensive care unit, day 3 after a revascularised inferior myocardial infarction. A 62-year-old man, stable, LVEF 45%. The discharge tracing is shown. Statement: this tracing contraindicates starting a beta-blocker.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: isolated, stable first-degree AV block is not a contraindication; a beta-blocker can be started at a low dose with PR monitoring.
Correct: only unpaced second- or third-degree AV block contraindicates beta-blockers; first-degree AV block simply calls for caution.
cas-ecgc-038.explication: Every P wave is conducted with a constant PR of about 280 ms and narrow QRS complexes: first-degree AV block. After inferior infarction, nodal PR prolongation is common (ischaemia or vagal tone) and often transient. Contraindications to beta-blockers include second- and third-degree AV block without a pacemaker, symptomatic bradycardia and decompensated heart failure. Here, if a beta-blocker is indicated after this infarction, it can be started at a low dose, with a follow-up ECG to monitor the PR and detect progression of the block.
cas-ecgc-038.aRetenir: Isolated first-degree AV block: not a contraindication to beta-blockers, but the PR should be monitored.
cas-ecgc-038.rappel: First-degree AV block (PR > 200 ms, all P waves conducted) is usually nodal, especially with narrow QRS complexes. After inferior infarction, nodal conduction disturbances are common and usually resolve. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in unpaced second- and third-degree AV block, not in isolated first-degree AV block, which warrants cautious initiation and ECG follow-up. A PR that lengthens markedly on treatment, or the appearance of blocked P waves, calls for reassessment.

cas-ecgc-039.question: Emergency department. An 84-year-old woman with a VVI pacemaker for complete AV block had a faint feeling while hanging out washing; sensing is unipolar. Here is the tracing recorded during the episode. Statement: a magnet placed over the generator during this episode would have prevented the pause.
options: True
False
commentaires: Correct: under a magnet the pacemaker paces in VOO without sensing; spurious signals can no longer inhibit pacing.
Incorrect: the pause is due to inhibition by oversensing, which is precisely what the magnet abolishes by disabling sensing.
cas-ecgc-039.explication: During the pause the baseline is noisy and no spike is delivered, while the P waves continue: pacemaker inhibition by oversensing, here probably of pectoral myopotentials during arm elevation with unipolar sensing. A magnet disables sensing and imposes asynchronous pacing: the pause would not have occurred. This is a temporary solution (transfer, monitoring, procedure); the definitive fix is to program bipolar sensing if the lead allows it, or a less sensitive setting with an adequate margin relative to the R wave. Provocative manoeuvres (arm movements) with electrogram recording confirm the diagnosis.
cas-ecgc-039.aRetenir: Pause due to oversensing: a magnet abolishes it temporarily; the definitive fix is bipolar sensing or a less sensitive setting.
cas-ecgc-039.rappel: Myopotential oversensing mainly affects leads programmed to unipolar sensing, whose sensing field includes the pectoral muscles next to the generator. It is reproduced by provocative manoeuvres (hand pressing, resisted arm adduction) during recording. Treatment is bipolar sensing or a less sensitive setting, while keeping a margin relative to the cardiac signal. A magnet disables sensing on a pacemaker and is a stopgap measure in dependent patients.

cas-ecgc-040.question: Exercise test. A 73-year-old woman has a pacemaker programmed to AAIR (lower rate 60 bpm, maximum sensor rate 140 bpm) for sinus node dysfunction with chronotropic incompetence. Here is the tracing at the 50 W stage. Statement: this tracing is enough to guarantee that AV conduction will remain 1:1 up to the maximum sensor rate.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: 1:1 conduction at 85 bpm says nothing about conduction at 140 bpm; the Wenckebach point may be reached earlier.
Correct: in AAIR, rate response speeds up the atrium without protecting the ventricle; if the Wenckebach point is below the maximum sensor rate, functional AV block will appear on exertion.
cas-ecgc-040.explication: Each spike is followed by a P wave and then a narrow conducted QRS: sensor-driven atrial pacing at 85 bpm with 1:1 AV conduction at this stage. This guarantees nothing at higher rates: as the atrial pacing rate increases, nodal conduction may reach its Wenckebach point, especially in the elderly or on rate-slowing drugs. In AAIR there is no ventricular backup pacing: the patient would develop Wenckebach or 2:1 block, with an abrupt fall in ventricular rate at peak exercise. Conduction must therefore be checked at the maximum sensor rate (incremental atrial pacing test at the programmer or maximal exercise) and, if necessary, that rate lowered or the device switched to DDDR with ventricular pacing minimisation.
cas-ecgc-040.aRetenir: In AAIR, check AV conduction at the maximum sensor rate: the Wenckebach point may be exceeded during exercise.
cas-ecgc-040.rappel: AAI(R) mode paces and senses the atrium only: it relies on dependable AV conduction, since nothing protects the ventricle. With rate response, the atrial pacing rate can reach values at which nodal conduction is no longer 1:1 (the Wenckebach point). The maximum sensor rate must therefore stay below the Wenckebach point, measured by incremental atrial pacing. Because of the risk of subsequent AV block in sinus node dysfunction, dual-chamber pacemakers with ventricular pacing minimisation algorithms are now preferred over pure AAI mode.
